newsitem.title: UK: British business chiefs criticise costs of EU.
newsitem.headline: British business chiefs criticise costs of EU.

text.p: Britain's debate over relations with the European Union (EU) took another twist on Friday as a group of 13 business figures criticised the "heavy costs" of membership in a letter to the Financial Times (FT).

Two days after a group led by British Airways Plc chairman Sir Colin Marshall called for a more positive attitude towards Europe in a letter to the FT, another group has used the same forum to slam uncritical attitudes towards the EU.
"Britain's interests in Europe will not be advanced by an attitude of uncritical acceptance," said the group, led by J. Chrisopher Miller, chief executive of industrial group Wassall Plc .

Criticising Marshall's letter for not mentioning the "heavy costs imposed on British industry" by the EU, it said the Union had become a "regulated bloc in which unnecessary rules, pushed by special interest groups, are imposed on all participating states."
It said the EU's Common Agricultural Policy artificially drove up prices and that the social chapter and single currency would add to business costs.
Only nine percent of the economy depends on trade with the EU, the letter argued, but the whole economy was "restricted by Brussels directives."

"Britain must be prepared to defend its interests robustly as a participant in the single market," the letter went on. "Dismissing any criticism as "extreme" does nothing for our negotiating position."

The division of view within British industry comes ahead of an election expected to be called for May 1 in which policies towards the EU and its planned single currency are likely to be a leading issue.
The opposition Labour party will be hoping to exploit dissent within the ruling Conservatives over EU policy but the debate within business highlights the complexities of the issues involved.

Wednesday's letter from Marshall and 22 others said they had "watched with dismay the spread of extreme Euroscepticism" and argued that Britain would suffer economically if it became more distanced from the EU.

Other signatories of Friday's letter included Sir Stanley Kalms, chairman of electrical retailer Dixons Group Plc , Burton Group Plc chairman Sir John Hoskyns and former Conservative minister Lord Young of Graffham.
